t: Guess the Number Using Bitwise Questions II — Query Each Bit Twice
o: Each call commonBits(num) reports how many bits n and num agree on, then XORs num into n. Calling it twice with the same num restores n (XOR is an involution) and yields two counts differing by exactly ±1 depending on the original bit: if bit i of n was 1, the first count includes it and the second does not, so first − second = +1; if it was 0, first − second = −1. Querying each of the 30 bit positions twice reconstructs n exactly. Example: for bit i set, counts differ by 1; cleared, by −1.
k: commonBits(num) twice with the same num leaves n unchanged (self-inverse XOR).
sign of (count₁ − count₂) reveals bit i of the original n.
30 bits ⇒ 60 calls total, well within interactive limits.

a.i: For each bit position i, call commonBits(1 << i) twice. The difference of the returned agreement counts is +1 iff bit i of the original n is set. Accumulate these bits into the answer.
s: For i in 0..29: a = commonBits(1 << i); b = commonBits(1 << i).
If a > b, set bit i in ans.
a.t: O(1) — exactly 60 API calls regardless of n.

w: The involution property (num XOR num = 0) is the entire trick — verify it aloud in an interview. Pitfall: calling with masks that touch multiple bits muddies the count difference; always query one isolated bit. Follow-up: minimize queries further (part I of this problem series uses a cleverer scheme); discuss information-theoretic lower bounds of 30 bits.
